claims.text: The investigated alloy has composition Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Melt-spinning this alloy at approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous structure.
The rapidly quenched initial state contains amorphous regions.
The rapidly quenched initial state contains embryonic crystalline nuclei formed during cooling.
Slow cooling of this alloy produces a complex microstructure containing several crystalline phases.
Accelerated cooling reduces the number of crystalline phases relative to slow cooling.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance the glass-forming ability of this alloy during very rapid cooling.
A brief isothermal hold at approximately Tg minus 50 K immediately after rapid cooling will promote structural relaxation.
Structural relaxation during the hold will place atoms into lower-energy configurations.
The hold-induced structural relaxation will passivate high-energy heterogeneous nucleation sites.
Passivation of high-energy nucleation sites will minimize atomic mobility and retard crystalline-phase formation and growth.
The hold will reduce the driving force for heterogeneous nucleation.
The intervention will increase the retained amorphous fraction relative to processing without the hold.
The intervention will reduce the formation of primary crystalline phases relative to processing without the hold.
The intervention will extend the amorphous stability window and shift the crystallization onset temperature Tx upward during reheating.
The intervention is effective at cooling rates exceeding approximately 10^4 K/s, including melt-spinning rates of 10^5–10^6 K/s.
A hold lasting only a few seconds at approximately Tg minus 50 K is sufficient to produce the predicted benefit.
The standard sequence of rapid cooling, slower cooling, and reheating results in significant primary crystallization and a multistep crystallization sequence.

contradictions.description: The intervention is applied at Tg minus 50 K after rapid quenching, where the material is described as containing amorphous regions, but the mechanism describes the atoms as being in a supercooled liquid. A temperature 50 K below Tg ordinarily corresponds to a glass rather than a supercooled liquid.
